content: Agnatha, derived from the Greek term meaning no jaws, is a paraphyletic superclass of jawless fish within the phylum Chordata and subphylum Vertebrata. This group has existed since the Cambrian period and continues to persist in modern times. The two extant groups of jawless fish, collectively referred to as cyclostomes, are lampreys and hagfish, comprising approximately 100 species in total. Although hagfish are classified within Vertebrata, they lack true vertebrae and are sometimes placed in the group Craniata instead. Agnathans are defined by several key characteristics. They lack jaws and paired fins, and they possess a notochord that persists throughout their entire life cycle, both in larval and adult stages. They have seven or more paired gill pouches and a light-sensitive pineal eye, which is homologous to the pineal gland found in mammals. Most living and extinct Agnathans lack a distinct stomach or any form of appendages. Reproduction involves external fertilization and development, with no parental care provided. Agnathans are ectothermic (cold-blooded) and have a cartilaginous skeleton. Their heart is composed of two chambers. Despite their superficial resemblance to one another, many of these features are considered basal traits of ancient vertebrates. Modern classifications often separate hagfish into the group Myxini (or Hyperotreti), while lampreys (Hyperoartii) are thought to be more closely related to jawed vertebrates. Respiratory System Agnathans possess seven or more pairs of gill pouches, which are supported by bronchial arches located close to the body surface. Metabolism Agnathans are ectothermic, meaning they rely on external environmental temperatures to regulate their body heat. As a result, their metabolic rate is slow, and they do not require large amounts of food. Additionally, they lack a stomach, which further influences their metabolic processes. Body Covering Modern Agnathans are covered only by skin and lack scales. However, extinct Agnathans were often protected by thick, bony plates. Appendages Agnathans do not have paired appendages, but they do possess a tail and a caudal fin. Skeleton The skeleton of Agnathans is cartilaginous, composed of dense connective tissue rather than bone. They retain a notochord throughout their life, which serves as a primitive vertebral column and is a defining feature of this class. Reproduction Fertilization and development in Agnathans occur externally. There is no evidence of parental care in this group. Fossil Agnathans Although Agnathans are a minor component of modern marine ecosystems, they were a dominant group of early fish during the Paleozoic era. Fossil evidence from the Early Cambrian Maotianshan shales in China includes two species, Haikouichthys and Myllokunmingia, which are believed to belong to Agnatha. Another possible Agnathan from the same region is Haikouella. Additionally, an undescribed potential Agnathan has been reported from the Middle Cambrian Burgess Shale in British Columbia. During the Ordovician, Silurian, and Devonian periods, many Agnathans were armored with heavy, bony, and spiky plates. The first armored Agnathans, known as Ostracoderms, are considered precursors to bony fish and, ultimately, to tetrapods, including humans. Ostracoderms first appeared in the Middle Ordovician and reached their evolutionary peak by the Late Silurian. However, Agnathans experienced a significant decline during the Devonian period and never fully recovered.
